solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Country and Western drinks

parts.note: W is the standard abbreviation for western, as on a compass
ales are beers, drinks served in a pub

explanation.surface: A request at a bar for country-and-western music and a round of drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country and Western' reads as the music genre, but 'Country' is the definition and 'Western' alone gives W.
explanation.definitionFit: Wales is one of the four nations making up the United Kingdom, a country in its own right.

clue.text: Fats Waller's rippling cascades

indicators.note: rippling suggests something moving in waves, so the letters of the name are stirred up

parts.note: the possessive 's adds no letter, leaving the surname as written

explanation.surface: The jazz pianist Fats Waller playing flowing runs on the keys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rippling' turns the ten letters of FATS WALLER into the answer; Fats Waller was an American jazz pianist, so the surface sounds like a music review.
explanation.definitionFit: Cascades are falls of water tumbling down rock, the plural synonym for these natural features.

clue.text: A golfer gets upset about first putt in game

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the shuffled letters go around the next piece
upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters of the two words are rearranged
first picks out the opening letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A golfer loses composure over the opening putt of a round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets upset' scrambles A GOLFER, and 'about' wraps those letters around the 'first' letter of 'putt'; the golf surface hides a playground game.
explanation.definitionFit: Leapfrog is a children's playground game in which players vault over each other's bent backs.

clue.text: Lengthens one's stride if stair treads are missing

explanation.surface: Someone striding out because the steps on a staircase have gone.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense reads the phrase literally: the steps are out, that is, absent.
explanation.definitionFit: To step out is to walk with longer, quicker strides; read literally, it says the stair treads are gone.

clue.text: Interior decoration, pretty as can be

indicators.note: can be suggests the letters may form something else, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Praise for a room's furnishings as being as pretty as possible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as can be' looks like a stock phrase, but 'can be' is the anagram signal for PRETTY AS.
explanation.definitionFit: A tapestry is a woven wall hanging, a classic item of decoration inside a house.

clue.text: Hazel pulled up a fish

indicators.note: in a down clue, pulled up means read from the bottom upwards, so the word is reversed

parts.note: a hazel is a nut, the tree and its fruit sharing the name

explanation.surface: A girl named Hazel landing a fish on her line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hazel' looks like a woman's name but is the nut, which 'pulled up' turns backwards in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuna is a large ocean fish, a familiar food fish, so it is a straightforward example.

clue.text: Become more relaxed when no longer criticised, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the answer is a word sounding like the phrase that follows

parts.note: ex- means former and panned means harshly reviewed, so ex-panned is no longer criticised

explanation.surface: Someone loosening up once the critics stop attacking them.
explanation.walkthrough: The homophone splits the answer into EX (formerly) and PANNED (slated by critics).
explanation.definitionFit: To expand is to open up and become more genial or talkative, an idiomatic sense of loosening up.

clue.text: Makes you French look Italian

parts.note: tu is the French word for you
to scan is to look over carefully

explanation.surface: A fashion remark that a French person can look Italian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Makes' is a link word joining the wordplay to the definition 'Italian'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuscan describes someone or something from Tuscany, a region of Italy, so it is an Italian of a kind.

clue.text: Distance vehicle travels uphill

indicators.note: in a down clue, travelling uphill means going from bottom to top, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a dray is a low cart, a brewer's vehicle

explanation.surface: How far a vehicle manages to climb up a slope.
explanation.walkthrough: A dray is a heavy horse-drawn cart used by brewers.
explanation.definitionFit: A yard is an imperial unit of length, so it is a measure of distance.

clue.text: Unusually strained exchanges

indicators.note: unusually means in an uncommon way, so the letters appear in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: Diplomatic talks that have become unusually tense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exchanges' suggests conversations, but it is the verb: to part-exchange an old item.
explanation.definitionFit: To trade in an old car is to hand it over as part payment, which is to exchange it.

clue.text: Lent is brought forward

explanation.surface: A note that the season before Easter is moved earlier this year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lent' looks like the season before Easter, but it is the past tense of lend, as money is advanced.
explanation.definitionFit: Money advanced is money lent ahead of time, and anything advanced has been moved forward.

clue.text: Drinks provided for men on board

explanation.surface: Drinks laid on for the crew of a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'men on board' suggests sailors, but means the pieces of a board game: draughts is the British name for checkers.
explanation.definitionFit: Draughts are gulps of liquid, and draughts are also the counters of the board game.

clue.text: No acceptance of FA rules being broken

indicators.note: broken means smashed apart, so the letters are reassembled in a new order

explanation.surface: Football Association regulations being flouted and not accepted.
explanation.walkthrough: FA is the Football Association, England's governing body for football; its letters join RULES as the anagram material.
explanation.definitionFit: A refusal is a rejection, the opposite of saying yes to something offered.

clue.text: Such tolerance may be a matter of degree

explanation.surface: A remark that leniency is always a question of how much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a matter of degree' means a question of extent, but here it is literal: latitude is measured in degrees north or south.
explanation.definitionFit: Latitude is freedom of action allowed by others, and also position measured in degrees from the equator.

clue.text: Deserted by Jack and done in

parts.note: a jack is a sailor, and AB (able seaman) is another

indicators.note: in places one word inside another, so the first is split open to hold it

explanation.surface: A man left alone by Jack and destroyed by it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'done in' looks like a phrase for exhausted; instead 'in' places the second word inside the first. 'by' is a link meaning next to.
explanation.definitionFit: Abandoned means left behind for good, exactly what deserted means of a person or place.

clue.text: You can have it yet still be clothes-mad

definitions.text: You can have it yet still be clothes-mad

parts.words: You can have it yet still be clothes-mad
parts.note: a good eye for what to wear can coexist with an obsession for buying garments, so being sensible about clothing need not mean being sane about them

explanation.surface: A wry remark that good taste in clothes does not stop someone being obsessed with them.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the contrast between 'sense' and 'mad': you can have good judgement about clothes and still be crazy about them.
explanation.definitionFit: Dress sense is an instinct for choosing flattering clothes, the judgement the clue allows a clothes-mad person.

clue.text: Discharge for sudden refusal to work

explanation.surface: A thunderstorm flash compared with a walkout that happens without warning.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a lightning strike is a walkout called with no notice.
explanation.definitionFit: A bolt of lightning hitting something is an electrical discharge, and an unannounced walkout by workers bears the same name.

clue.text: Don't be in a hurry to use a stop-watch

explanation.surface: Advice to slow down, then to time something with a stop-watch.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense reads literally: to take the time of something is to measure it.
explanation.definitionFit: To take time over something is to do it unhurriedly, and to take the time of a race is to clock it.

clue.text: Offering hospitality is attractive

explanation.surface: A host's welcome described as appealing.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is the verb form, asking guests round; the second is the adjective, tempting.
explanation.definitionFit: Inviting is asking people to come as guests, and an inviting prospect is a tempting one.

clue.text: Special outfit for a round-the-world trip?

definitions.text: Special outfit for a round-the-world trip?

parts.words: Special outfit for a round-the-world trip?
parts.note: a round-the-world trip suggests a long holiday, but here it means orbiting the planet, which needs a pressurised garment

explanation.surface: Asking what to pack for a world tour holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round-the-world trip' suggests a gap-year holiday, but here it means orbiting the Earth.
explanation.definitionFit: An astronaut's pressurised garment is worn to circle the Earth, a special outfit for orbital travel.

clue.text: Nearly a fifty majority

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
most means the greater part, the majority

explanation.surface: A description of an election result just short of a fifty majority.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a parliamentary majority of fifty, but L is the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Almost and nearly are synonyms, both meaning not quite but very close to.

clue.text: It's sufficient to upset one with an expression of disgust

indicators.note: upset means overturned, so the letters of the short word are jumbled

parts.note: ugh is an exclamation of revulsion

explanation.surface: Someone who has had enough after being upset by a person grunting in disgust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to upset' jumbles the short word; 'It's' and 'with' are link words, and the definition is 'sufficient' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Enough and sufficient both mean as much as is needed and no more.

clue.text: Sort Eastern spices out

indicators.note: out means put out of order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An instruction to sort oriental spices from a cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort' looks like a verb telling you to sort the spices, but it is the noun meaning kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A species is a kind or type, the noun sense of sort, as in a different sort of person.

clue.text: Drunk, a mob jeer a troopers' rally

indicators.note: drunk means intoxicated and staggering, so the letters reel into a new order

explanation.surface: A drunken mob jeering at a gathering of soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troopers' sounds like soldiers, but means scouts, whose troops meet at international rallies.
explanation.definitionFit: A jamboree is a large gathering of Scouts, whose units are called troops, so a rally of troopers.

clue.text: Imprison the Italian after German agreement

indicators.note: after says the Italian piece follows the German one in the answer

parts.note: ja is the German word for yes
il is the Italian for the

explanation.surface: Putting an Italian behind bars following a German treaty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'agreement' suggests a treaty, but here it is just a German yes.
explanation.definitionFit: To jail someone is to lock them up in prison, the verb sense of the word.

clue.text: It's not difficult to name a novel midshipman

explanation.surface: A remark that naming a fictional naval cadet is simple.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Midshipman Easy is an 1836 novel by Captain Frederick Marryat; 'It's' and 'to' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy means requiring little effort, and it is also the surname of Marryat's fictional young naval officer.

clue.text: Sound proof of what a performer can do

definitions.text: proof of what a performer can do

explanation.surface: An actor's tryout described as a demonstration of skill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound proof' suggests soundproof, but splits: audition can mean the faculty of hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Audition is the sense of hearing, and an audition is a trial performance showing an actor's or singer's ability.

clue.text: Entrance qualification for Yale?

parts.note: Yale suggests the American university and its admissions, but it is also a lock brand, so getting in needs a door opener

explanation.surface: A question about the requirements for admission to Yale University.
explanation.walkthrough: Yale is the university, but also a brand of cylinder lock common on British front doors.
explanation.definitionFit: A Yale lock is opened by its own small key, the qualification needed to get through the front door.

clue.text: Bird — but not birdie

explanation.surface: A golfer correcting someone about which bird name applies to a score.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf a birdie is one under par and an eagle two under, so the score better than a birdie is this one.
explanation.definitionFit: An eagle is a large bird of prey, and in golf it is the score of two under par, beating a birdie.
